checkpoints: Implement /register and /login in Flask that return JWT tokens
Store the token in React state (not localStorage) for this stage
Attach the token to every protected API request
Handle 401 responses in React by redirecting to login
Implement logout by clearing the token from state

content.value: Authentication requires coordination between both layers. Flask issues a JWT on login; React stores it and sends it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header on every subsequent request. Use an axios instance with a request interceptor: axiosInstance.interceptors.request.use(config => { config.headers.Authorization = 'Bearer ' + token; return config; }). When a request returns 401, a response interceptor can automatically redirect to the login page. Store the token in React state (or Zustand) rather than localStorage to avoid XSS risks — the trade-off is that the session doesn't survive a page refresh, which you'll address with refresh tokens later.

checkpoints: Create a PrivateRoute wrapper component
Redirect unauthenticated users to /login
Preserve the intended destination URL in state
Redirect back to the intended page after login

content.value: Not all pages should be accessible to unauthenticated users. Create a PrivateRoute component that checks for a token — if absent, redirects to /login using React Router's Navigate. Pass the current location to the redirect: <Navigate to='/login' state={{ from: location }} />. In the Login component, after successful authentication, read state.from and navigate there: navigate(state?.from || '/'). This gives users a seamless experience — they land on the page they originally intended to visit. Pair this with a public-only route wrapper that redirects authenticated users away from /login.

checkpoints: Install Flask-SocketIO and set up a WebSocket server
Connect to the WebSocket from React using socket.io-client
Emit and receive events between client and server
Build a live counter or chat feature to verify real-time updates
Handle disconnect and reconnect gracefully

content.value: HTTP is request-response: the client asks, the server answers. WebSockets are persistent, bidirectional connections — the server can push data to the client without being asked. Flask-SocketIO adds WebSocket support. On the server: @socketio.on('message') def handle_message(data): socketio.emit('response', data). On the client: const socket = io('http://localhost:5000'); socket.on('response', data => setMessages([...messages, data])). Build a simple live chat room: every message sent by any user is broadcast to all connected clients instantly. This architecture underpins collaborative features, live dashboards, and notifications.

moduleTitle: File Uploads from React to Flask
checkpoints: Build a file input in React with preview for images
Send the file as FormData via a POST fetch
Validate and save the file in Flask
Return the file URL and display the uploaded image in React

content.value: File uploads use multipart/form-data, not JSON. In React: const formData = new FormData(); formData.append('avatar', file); fetch('/api/upload', { method: 'POST', body: formData }). Don't set Content-Type manually — the browser sets the multipart boundary automatically. In Flask: file = request.files['avatar']. Validate the extension and size, save with secure_filename, and return the relative URL. In React, display the returned URL in an tag. For a polished UX, show a preview before upload using URL.createObjectURL(file).

moduleTitle: State Management with Zustand Across Pages
checkpoints: Create a Zustand store with user auth state
Persist the auth token to sessionStorage via the persist middleware
Access user state from any page without prop drilling
Reset the store on logout

content.value: As your app grows, React state in a top-level component and prop drilling becomes unwieldy. Zustand centralizes auth state: the user object, the token, and the login/logout actions live in one store. Any component reads state with useAuthStore(state => state.user) — no props needed. Use the persist middleware with sessionStorage as the storage engine so the session survives a page refresh but not a browser close (a reasonable security trade-off for most apps). The logout action clears the store and sessionStorage simultaneously. This pattern scales cleanly to apps with dozens of pages.

checkpoints: Add page and per_page query parameters to a Flask list endpoint
Return metadata: total, page, per_page, has_next
Implement page-based pagination controls in React
Alternatively, implement infinite scroll using an Intersection Observer

content.value: Large datasets can't be returned all at once. Add pagination to Flask: page = request.args.get('page', 1, type=int); items = Item.query.paginate(page=page, per_page=20). Return total count and has_next in the response. In React, numbered pagination buttons call the API with the new page number and replace the current list. Infinite scroll is more engaging: use an IntersectionObserver to detect when the user reaches the bottom of the list and automatically append the next page. TanStack Query's useInfiniteQuery makes the infinite scroll pattern significantly cleaner to implement.

checkpoints: Users register and log in; sessions managed with JWT in Zustand
Authenticated users can create, edit, and delete bookmarks
Bookmark list has pagination or infinite scroll
Protected routes redirect unauthenticated users to login
Users can upload a profile avatar
Deploy the full stack and test end-to-end

content.value: Your capstone is a multi-user app that requires authentication, protected routes, file uploads, and pagination — all coordinated between a Flask API and a React frontend. This is the complexity level of real production software. Plan the API endpoints first (a simple table of method, path, auth required, description), then build the Flask layer, then the React layer. Test the full user journey: register → log in → create bookmarks → upload avatar → log out → confirm bookmarks persist. Deploy and share the live URL.
